steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on lip-to-speech synthesis for any speaker in the wild, where the idea is to use the output of a pre-trained lip-to-text model to help generate speech. Motivate the task, explain why existing work falls short, and finish with a short contributions subsection.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Lip reading: why it matters and where it is used
- Lip-to-speech vs. lip-to-text: why speech is the more valuable output
- Why lip-to-speech is hard and where existing models fall short
- Our Contributions: key idea and approach
- Contribution list

  - our work: speech for silent lip movements of an ALS patient (not shown before); people with hearing loss

  - must distill content from lips AND model speaker attributes (voice, accent, style)
  - until recently: single-speaker or constrained multi-speaker, limited corpus and vocabulary (cite)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Humans are multi-sensory beings, we experience the world through many senses and we adapt to make the most of what we perceive. If one sense like hearing is diminished, the brain relies more on other senses like vision, so that the person can stay independent and navigate the environment. For deaf people, one of the most common ways to understand speech is lip reading, which means understanding what is said only from silent lip movements. So lip reading has many applications, from searching through old silent films to assistive technology for people who cannot speak. For example, people with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) often lose the ability to speak because of problems with their vocal cords, but they can still mouth words. So developing automated lip reading technology can improve the communication abilities of people with ALS. In the past few years previous works have shown that lip reading is much easier for deep learning models than for humans. There is a growing interest in the research community in transcribing silent lip movements into text. But while big progress is being made in lip-to-text generation, only a few works go further and generate speech from silent lip movements. The gap between these two closely related tasks is getting more and more evident. Lip-to-text models now reach word error rates as low as 17\% WER, but there are no lip-to-speech systems that are usable in practice and generate natural, meaningful speech for in-the-wild identities.

Lip-to-Speech generation is more exciting and more challenging, and it also has more far-reaching applications. For example, a live video call with a person who has lost their voice is more engaging than reading a text transcription of their silent lip movements. Speech also conveys more than text: if the silent lip movements are converted to speech and not to text, it is possible to express emotions. Speech is also more instantaneous for the listener, because hearing is easier and faster than reading text. This immersive user experience is a big motivation for developing algorithms that translate lip movements directly to speech. Lip-to-Speech can also be used in forensic investigations, where silent footage is analyzed to find out what was said, or to generate speech from archival film footage. Our work shows the practical impact of lip-to-speech generation by generating speech for the silent lip movements of an ALS patient, which other models in this field have not demonstrated before. We also show results on reading the mouth movements of people with hearing loss, to show further that accurate lip-to-speech synthesis is effective. More details about the applications are in Section 4.3.

  - until recently: single-speaker or constrained multi-speaker, limited corpus and vocabulary (cite)
  - recent in-the-wild efforts (cite) mostly speaker-specific
  - speaker-independent models (cite) fail on language and speech attributes (voice, prosody); below expectations for end users
## Our Contributions
  - goal: speech for silent lip video of any speaker in the wild, in any target voice
  - premise: current models learn language + speech only from speech supervision; ignore lip-to-text advances
  - lip-to-speech without text supervision very hard -> unclear, unintelligible outputs in unconstrained settings
  - key idea: lip-to-text models already extract content from lips (text supervision)
  - use silent video + noisy text transcriptions from pre-trained lip-to-text model
  - train a visual text-to-speech model, speech in sync with input video
  - outperforms existing multi-speaker lip-to-speech models, qualitative + quantitative

  - (2) visual TTS model synced with video; beats multi-speaker baselines

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Humans are multi-sensory beings, we experience the world through many senses and we adapt to make the most of what we perceive. If one sense like hearing is diminished, the brain relies more on other senses like vision, so that the person can stay independent and navigate the environment. For deaf people, one of the most common ways to understand speech is lip reading, which means understanding what is said only from silent lip movements. So lip reading has many applications, from searching through old silent films to assistive technology for people who cannot speak. For example, people with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) often lose the ability to speak because of problems with their vocal cords, but they can still mouth words. So developing automated lip reading technology can improve the communication abilities of people with ALS. In the past few years previous works have shown that lip reading is much easier for deep learning models than for humans. There is a growing interest in the research community in transcribing silent lip movements into text. But while big progress is being made in lip-to-text generation, only a few works go further and generate speech from silent lip movements. The gap between these two closely related tasks is getting more and more evident. Lip-to-text models now reach word error rates as low as 17\% WER, but there are no lip-to-speech systems that are usable in practice and generate natural, meaningful speech for in-the-wild identities.

Lip-to-Speech generation is more exciting and more challenging, and it also has more far-reaching applications. For example, a live video call with a person who has lost their voice is more engaging than reading a text transcription of their silent lip movements. Speech also conveys more than text: if the silent lip movements are converted to speech and not to text, it is possible to express emotions. Speech is also more instantaneous for the listener, because hearing is easier and faster than reading text. This immersive user experience is a big motivation for developing algorithms that translate lip movements directly to speech. Lip-to-Speech can also be used in forensic investigations, where silent footage is analyzed to find out what was said, or to generate speech from archival film footage. Our work shows the practical impact of lip-to-speech generation by generating speech for the silent lip movements of an ALS patient, which other models in this field have not demonstrated before. We also show results on reading the mouth movements of people with hearing loss, to show further that accurate lip-to-speech synthesis is effective. More details about the applications are in Section 4.3.

However, synthesizing speech from silent talking-face videos is much more challenging than lip-to-text generation. The model first needs to get the content from the lip movements, and then it also needs to generate the final speech by accurately modeling speaker attributes like voice, accent, and style. Because of these difficulties, until recently most of the existing works focused on single-speaker models or on constrained multi-speaker models with limited corpus size and limited vocabulary. More recent efforts like have extended lip-to-speech to "in-the-wild" environments, but most of these models are speaker-specific, so they only work on the speakers they were trained on. The speaker-independent models have many weaknesses and fail to accurately learn language and speech attributes like voice, prosody, etc. Because the task is so difficult, they end up well below expectations for an end-user application.

## Our Contributions

Our goal is to generate speech for a silent lip video of any speaker in the wild, and in any desired target voice. The main premise of this paper is that current models for this task struggle to learn language and speech attributes, because they try to learn both of them only from speech supervision. They disregard the advancements that were made in the sibling task of lip-to-text generation. We argue that learning lip-to-speech without any understanding or supervision of text is very hard, and this can be seen in all the current models, which fail to produce clear and intelligible outputs in unconstrained settings. Our key idea is that lip-to-text models have already learned to extract content from lips, because they are trained with text supervision. We show that using the silent video input and the noisy text transcriptions from a pre-trained lip-to-text model gives accurate, natural, and high-quality speech outputs. We train a visual text-to-speech model that synthesizes speech in sync with the input video. Our approach outperforms the existing multi-speaker lip-to-speech models by a large margin in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. Our key contributions are below.

- (1) Lip-to-Speech generation is hard with only speech supervision, and current models struggle to learn language and speech attributes. So we propose to use the output of a pre-trained lip-to-text model to help lip-to-speech generation.

- (2) We train a visual text-to-speech model to synthesize speech that is in sync with the input video. With this we outperform existing multi-speaker lip-to-speech models in qualitative and quantitative evaluations.

- (3) Our approach gives accurate and natural speech output for silent lip videos of any speaker in any desired target voice.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
As multi-sensory beings, humans can experience the world through various senses, adapting to make the most of what we perceive. When one sense, like hearing, is diminished, the brain compensates by relying more on other senses, like vision, to maintain independence and navigate the environment. One of the most prevalent ways for deaf individuals to comprehend speech is lip reading - understanding spoken content purely from silent lip movements. Lip reading therefore has numerous applications, ranging from searching through old silent films to assistive technology for people who are unable to speak. For example, people with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) often lose their ability to speak due to issues with their vocal cords but can still mouth words. Developing automated lip reading technologies can thus improve the communication abilities of people with ALS. In the past few years, previous works have shown that it is far easier for deep learning models to perform lip reading than it is for humans [1], and there has been a growing interest in the research community [2,3,4,1] in transcribing silent lip movements into text. While giant strides are being made in lip-to-text generation, only a handful of works go a step further and generate speech from silent lip movements, and the gap between these two closely related tasks is becoming increasingly evident. While lip-to-text models are reaching word error rates as low as 17\% WER [5], there are no practically usable lip-to-speech systems that generate natural, meaningful speech for in-the-wild identities.

Lip-to-Speech generation is not only more exciting and challenging but also has more far-reaching applications. For instance, a live video call with a person who has lost their voice is more engaging than reading the text transcription of their silent lip movements. Speech can convey more: emotions can be expressed through silent lip movements if they are converted to speech rather than text. Speech is also more instantaneous for the listener, since it is easier and faster to hear than to read text. This immersive user experience is a significant impetus for developing algorithms that translate lip movements directly to speech. Lip-to-Speech can also be applied in forensic investigations, where silent footage can be analyzed to determine what was being said, or to generate speech from archival film footage. Our work showcases the practical impact of lip-to-speech generation by generating speech for the silent lip movements of an ALS patient, which has not previously been demonstrated by other models in this field. We also show results on reading the mouth movements of people suffering from hearing loss to further demonstrate the effectiveness of accurate lip-to-speech synthesis. More details about the applications can be found in Section 4.3.

However, synthesizing speech from silent talking-face videos is far more challenging than lip-to-text generation. The model not only needs to distill the content from the lip movements, but also needs to generate the final speech by accurately modeling speaker attributes like voice, accent, and style. Owing to these difficulties, until recently most of the existing works [6,7,8] focused on building either single-speaker models or constrained multi-speaker models with limited corpus size and limited vocabulary. While more recent efforts like [8] have extended lip-to-speech to "in-the-wild" environments, most of these models are speaker-specific, i.e., they only work on the speakers they are trained on. The speaker-independent models [9,10,11,12] suffer from numerous weaknesses and fail to accurately learn language and speech attributes like voice, prosody, etc. Due to the difficulty of the task, they turn out to be well below expectations for an end-user application.

## 1.1. Our Contributions

First, we would like to state clearly that our goal is to generate speech for a silent lip video of any speaker in the wild and in any desired target voice. The fundamental premise of this paper is that current models trying to solve this task struggle to learn language and speech attributes because they try to learn both solely from speech supervision, inadvertently disregarding the advancements made in the sibling task of lip-to-text generation. We argue that learning lip-to-speech without any understanding/supervision of text is very challenging, as can be observed in all the current models, which fail to produce clear and intelligible outputs in unconstrained settings. Our key idea is to use the fact that lip-to-text models have already learned the task of extracting content from lips, as they are trained with text supervision. We show that we can achieve accurate, natural, and high-quality speech outputs by using the silent video input and the noisy text transcriptions from a pre-trained lip-to-text model. We train a visual text-to-speech model to synthesize speech that syncs with the input video. Our approach outperforms the existing multi-speaker lip-to-speech models by a significant margin in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. Our key contributions are highlighted below.

- (1) Lip-to-Speech generation is challenging with only speech supervision, and current models struggle to learn language and speech attributes. To address this, we propose using the output of a pre-trained lip-to-text model to aid lip-to-speech generation.

- (2) Our approach trains a visual text-to-speech model to synthesize speech that syncs with the input video. With this approach, we outperform existing multi-speaker lip-to-speech models in qualitative and quantitative evaluations.

- (3) Our approach enables accurate and natural speech output for silent lip videos of any speaker in any desired target voice.
